query: Hey folks, might be a dumb question but what are the main things that mess up ATS parsing? I know we've talked about resume formatting before and I'm trying to help someone on my team fix theirs
chunk_content:
Hi <@UC364AM7U>

• Professional summary is very big. HRs or hiring managers will not be able to find anything in it as it is more to read. Try to keep it in 2-3 lines if possible.
• Education: With 6+ exp, your education can be concise.
    ◦ No need to mention specialization.
    ◦ Try to keep it in 2 lines each education. 
    ◦ Please remove graduated with first class. Skill matter as you may know. 
• Professional experience: 
    ◦ Please remove Italic or bold fonts. 
    ◦ ATS will add star marks at prefix and suffix of any font style and it will not capture information properly.
    ◦ Bullet points are 2 liners in your entire experience.
    ◦ Only 50% or less in your entire resume should have bullet points that are more than 1line. 
    ◦ Use Impact> Action> Task format for your bullet points in the format.
    ◦ Do not end any points will numbers as the ATS parser will return with && and it will kill the formatting.
• Skills: 
    ◦ Skills on the top before your education or experience. 
    ◦ Keep in this order for clear visual.
    ◦ Summary> Skills>Education>Certification.
    ◦ Add certifications in one line each with awarding body.
• Language: 
    ◦ No need to mention languages.
    ◦ No one cares about native language.
    ◦ English is expected in today's world.
    ◦ Portuguese - Put on top near your address or somewhere or maybe include this as a liner in your summary.
    ◦ No need to mention any additional information as it is clearly evident in the resume. 
When asked, you can talk about career break. If you mention all points it will be difficult to talk something new in the interview. Try to keep your resume to one page. If not, 1.5 max. Too much of information most of the times go unread. Your aim to make the people catch their on your resume in 6-10 seconds of time. Don't use passive voice sentences. Try to use action verbs with string words to lead the points.

Biggest red flag for ATS:
Any sentence ending with numbers or symbols and placing a full stop will do symantic error with &&&& kind and it will miss the opportunity to read for others who check the resume.
validation_reason: The message directly answers the query about what messes up ATS parsing by providing detailed formatting guidelines and specific issues that cause ATS problems, including font styles (bold/italic), bullet point formatting, and sentences ending with numbers/symbols. The response is comprehensive and specifically focused on ATS-related resume formatting issues.

query: how do i fix my resume for ats parsing and what order shoudl skills/certs/edu go in
chunk_content:
Resume format is really good. Few identifiers:

• As I always say, skills go on top. 
• Followed by certifications> Education.
• Only most recent two educations are sufficient.
• Difficult to find break in your skills, Rather than using comma use bar symbol. It goes well with ATS.
• No need to mention projects if it is outside work exp. This will make hiring managers panic on stability. If it is within the job duties, mention in that relevant company. 
• Certifications or education wherever you are mentioning dates, always go in reverse chronological order. I see it is missing in your certifications.
• Try to remove any points that do not have any numbers. I mean to say any significant outcomes. If those are generic items like stakeholder management. It is already expectation on job duties. For example this point: 
    ◦ `Negotiated timelines with leadership and stakeholders, ensuring efficient product execution.`
• This is the expectation for a PM in their primary job duties. 
• Looks like resume has different fonts. Try to bring it one font all together. 
• No Italic on resume: This will not parse properly to the ATS.
Rest all is picture perfect.
validation_reason: The message directly addresses both parts of the query - it provides specific guidance on ATS parsing (use bar symbols instead of commas, avoid italics, use consistent fonts) and explicitly states the preferred order of sections (skills on top, followed by certifications, then education)

    ◦ Keep it to 2-3 lines.

    ◦ It is difficult to find where is your resume starting.
    ◦ Sub headings are mixed in the size of font on your resume.

    ◦ One line is sufficient for your education.

    ◦ Are these certificates you selected? Or who?

    ◦ This section is not at all required.

chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
Can someone help review my cv. I am finding it hard to get interview calls. Here is my attached. Thank you for reviewing and providing feedback.

[Reply by unknown]
Hi <@UC364AM7U>

• Professional summary is very big. HRs or hiring managers will not be able to find anything in it as it is more to read. Try to keep it in 2-3 lines if possible.
• Education: With 6+ exp, your education can be concise.
    ◦ No need to mention specialization.
    ◦ Try to keep it in 2 lines each education. 
    ◦ Please remove graduated with first class. Skill matter as you may know. 
• Professional experience: 
    ◦ Please remove Italic or bold fonts. 
    ◦ ATS will add star marks at prefix and suffix of any font style and it will not capture information properly.
    ◦ Bullet points are 2 liners in your entire experience.
    ◦ Only 50% or less in your entire resume should have bullet points that are more than 1line. 
    ◦ Use Impact> Action> Task format for your bullet points in the format.
    ◦ Do not end any points will numbers as the ATS parser will return with && and it will kill the formatting.
• Skills: 
    ◦ Skills on the top before your education or experience. 
    ◦ Keep in this order for clear visual.
    ◦ Summary> Skills>Education>Certification.
    ◦ Add certifications in one line each with awarding body.
• Language: 
    ◦ No need to mention languages.
    ◦ No one cares about native language.
    ◦ English is expected in today's world.
    ◦ Portuguese - Put on top near your address or somewhere or maybe include this as a liner in your summary.
    ◦ No need to mention any additional information as it is clearly evident in the resume. 
When asked, you can talk about career break. If you mention all points it will be difficult to talk something new in the interview. Try to keep your resume to one page. If not, 1.5 max. Too much of information most of the times go unread. Your aim to make the people catch their on your resume in 6-10 seconds of time. Don't use passive voice sentences. Try to use action verbs with string words to lead the points.

Biggest red flag for ATS:
Any sentence ending with numbers or symbols and placing a full stop will do symantic error with &&&& kind and it will miss the opportunity to read for others who check the resume.

query:
I'm conducting a comprehensive review of our organization's recruitment technology stack and compliance procedures, specifically examining our Applicant Tracking System (ATS) implementation and usage patterns. I need to validate our current practices against industry standards and regulatory requirements (particularly EEOC guidelines regarding human review of applications).

Context:
- We're currently evaluating three ATS vendors for potential migration
- Our compliance team has raised questions about automated screening capabilities
- We've received conflicting vendor claims about "AI-powered resume screening" and "ATS compliance optimization"
- I need to document actual ATS functionality vs. vendor marketing claims for our security and compliance review

What I've already investigated:
1. Reviewed vendor documentation from Greenhouse, Lever, and Workday
2. Examined EEOC technical assistance documents on automated employment decision tools
3. Consulted our legal team regarding 41 CFR 60-1.12 (recordkeeping requirements)

Specific information needed:
Can someone with direct hiring manager experience confirm the actual role of ATS systems in resume screening workflows? Specifically:
- Do ATS platforms automatically filter/reject candidates, or do they only assist human reviewers?
- What is the legal requirement for human review of applications in US hiring processes?
- Are vendor claims about "ATS-compliant resume formatting" technically valid, or is this marketing terminology without technical basis?
- What specific functionality do ATS systems actually provide to recruiters (keyword search, filtering capabilities, etc.)?

This information is needed to complete our vendor risk assessment and ensure our procurement decision aligns with both compliance requirements and operational security best practices.
chunk_content:
[Original Message by unknown]
I am an experienced hiring manager and have worked with many recruiters.  I would like to dispel a myth.  ATS does NOT pick resumes.  At least in the US, all resumes must be reviewed by a human.  ATS can  be used to assist the human in finding keywords, which are mostly specific technical words like "Python" or "Salesforce".  ATS are NOT used to match words like "team player".   There is a lot of misinformation from people who don't know how things work or from companies trying to sell snake oil with "ATS compliant" resumes.  THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS "ATS compliant"!  Hope that helps.

Hi there everyone — I am thinking through common LLM capabilities that are most often used when creating AI-enabled features in software apps. • *Explanation*: Rephrase input text address a selected audience while remaining accurate; may include summarization, though required.

• *Sentiment*:  Similar to tagging, primarily looking at the style + tonality of the input text versus the factual content itself.
Do these represent what your AI features address? What am I missing?

Hi there everyone — I am thinking through common LLM capabilities that are most often used when creating AI-enabled features in software apps.  I know every software app, esp. enterprise software, have their own requirements and features to support users.  But in the end, I have a sense that many of those features that leverage AI are actually rather similar when distilled down.

Here’s my list so far:

• *Data extraction*: Capturing from unstructured text into a object (e.g. JSON object) using a template/schema
• *Spam or malicious content detection*
• *Summarize (reduction):* Reducing a larger set of text into a content that highlights the key points.
• *Explanation*: Rephrase input text address a selected audience while remaining accurate; may include summarization, though required.
• *Content Tagging*: Apply tags for text using predefined tags, and/or define new tags based on configured criteria.
• *Content Translation*: Translate content into another language(s)
• *Sentiment*:  Similar to tagging, primarily looking at the style + tonality of the input text versus the factual content itself.
Do these represent what your AI features address? What am I missing?

Hey all!

I’ve been tinkering on this idea during parental leave.
Problem: 
Most first-time engineering managers (including me) face the same painful reality: leadership is trial-and-error. Whether it’s giving tough feedback, handling disengaged ICs, or pushing back on product priorities, mistakes cost teams morale and companies productivity. Current options for new EMs are books, courses or coaching. None of these provide safe, repeatable practice for real-world situations. That’s the gap NgLead fills.

Solution (prototype): I built NgLead, a flight simulator for engineering managers.
 – Face short, real-world scenarios (e.g. “your star IC starts slipping”).
 – Choose how you’d respond.
 – Get feedback + see how peers handled it.

The goal: let managers safely “get reps” in the hardest conversations before they have to do it live.

Ask:
As leaders/PMs, does this resonate as a real gap?
From a business perspective, what do you see as risks with this approach?

Prototype’s live at <http://nglead.org|nglead.org>. I can also share demo credentials if anyone wants to try it without signing up. Appreciate any feedback or feel free to DM me!

Hey all!

I’ve been tinkering on this idea during parental leave.
Problem: 
Most first-time engineering managers (including me) face the same painful reality: leadership is trial-and-error. Whether it’s giving tough feedback, handling disengaged ICs, or pushing back on product priorities, mistakes cost teams morale and companies productivity. Current options for new EMs are books, courses or coaching. None of these provide safe, repeatable practice for real-world situations. That’s the gap NgLead fills.

Solution (prototype): I built NgLead, a flight simulator for engineering managers.
 – Face short, real-world scenarios (e.g. “your star IC starts slipping”).
 – Choose how you’d respond.
 – Get feedback + see how peers handled it.

The goal: let managers safely “get reps” in the hardest conversations before they have to do it live.

Ask:
As leaders/PMs, does this resonate as a real gap?
From a business perspective, what do you see as risks with this approach?

Prototype’s live at <http://nglead.org|nglead.org>. I can also share demo credentials if anyone wants to try it without signing up. Appreciate any feedback or feel free to DM me!

Developed a framework for deciding what operations to integrate AI into. Thought I'd share it here. You can learn more in our free lightning lesson coming up this Friday: <https://maven.com/p/3cb375/how-to-build-an-agent-native-workplace>

Here's a framework for identifying where generative AI actually drives value:
1. Map your current operations with surgical precision. Decompose each workflow into granular tasks. Surface every implicit decision point in your processes.
2. Evaluate each micro-task individually. Deploy traditional software when:
- The process follows identical steps every time
- Accuracy is mission-critical
- Speed and efficiency trump creative variation
- You're integrating with established enterprise systems

DON'T USE AI

Deploy generative AI when:
- No existing software solution addresses the challenge
- You're processing unstructured human language or messy datasets
- Creative interpretation creates competitive advantage
- Near-perfect accuracy is acceptable (not mandatory)

Maybe your traditional software isn't perfect. But at least its predictable. It's an old friend whom you accepted with all the quirks and flaws. You know what you're getting into.

Generative AI applications are unpredictable by design. There is no bug to fix and sleep soundly. Everything is a statistical game. The winning mindset is: don't start playing that game unless you really have to.

[Message by unknown at 41409166-d588-53f6-9525-d25d2332a6fa]
Current wave of Ai tools are focusing on PD generations and/or summarizing customer interviews.... I think there is more to that when it comes to product management

• *Strategic Planning & Roadmap*
    ◦ Conduct quarterly OKR-setting sessions and align on top priorities.
    ◦ Maintain and socialize the product roadmap, updating as priorities shift.
    ◦ Run discovery sprints to validate new ideas and score them using RICE (Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort).
• Metrics & Performance
    ◦ Morning check of core dashboards: DAU/MAU, feature adoption, funnel conversion, churn rates.
    ◦ Weekly deep-dives on A/B tests and retention curves.
    ◦ Monthly P&L review with Finance, focusing on ARPU, LTV, and pricing experiments.
• Customer & Feedback Loop
    ◦ Schedule customer interviews monthly; summarize key pain points and wishes.
    ◦ Track NPS drivers and urgent support escalations in a shared dashboard.
    ◦ Host weekly “Voice of the Customer” review with Marketing, Design, and Engineering.
• *Marketing & Sales Enablement*
    ◦ Create sales playbooks, battle cards, and demo scripts for each major feature.
    ◦ Coordinate launch campaigns: emails, webinars, blog posts.
    ◦ Monitor campaign KPIs (opens, clicks, demo requests) and iterate messaging.
• *Weekly Rhythm*
    ◦ *Daily:* Dashboard review; stand-up; unblock engineers.
    ◦ *Weekly:* Deep metric review; stakeholder status emails; support triage.
    ◦ *Bi-Weekly:* Sprint planning; cross-functional sync.
    ◦ *Monthly:* Business review; roadmap checkpoint.

FIXING THE PRODUCT MANAGEMENT/SALES RELATIONSHIP
--------

We ran a survey and got some good data on problems Product Managers face in their jobs.

Interestingly, the 3 of the top 4 problems are tied to their relationship with the sales team.

• Working in a Sales-led org - individual deals impact product direction
• Large customers have unfair influence on product direction
• Lack of strategy beyond “more revenue”

So, we decided to address this problem. I create the *Reboot your Sales Relationship workshop* with Jason Knight, specifically designed to help B2B Product Managers and Leaders create a more effective and less stressful relationship with their sales teams.

[Message by unknown at 0cab81b8-692d-51f8-92cb-ce28e58d3a8a]
FIXING THE PRODUCT MANAGEMENT/SALES RELATIONSHIP
--------

We ran a survey and got some good data on problems Product Managers face in their jobs.

Interestingly, the 3 of the top 4 problems are tied to their relationship with the sales team.

• Working in a Sales-led org - individual deals impact product direction
• Large customers have unfair influence on product direction
• Lack of strategy beyond “more revenue”
This is an evergreen problem that most Product teams face. Sales has a huge footprint and amount of influence in many companies, and Product Manager (and Product leaders) are NOT trained on how to deal with this challenge.

So, we decided to address this problem. I create the *Reboot your Sales Relationship workshop* with Jason Knight, specifically designed to help B2B Product Managers and Leaders create a more effective and less stressful relationship with their sales teams.

Here’s what some previous student have said:

_“Highly practical course for product people aiming to navigate the complex yet essential relationship with Sales. The deep dives into ICP development and managing sales-led feature requests stand out. The final 1:1 session with Saeed was a highlight.”_

_Topics covered include:_

• How Sales Teams Work and Why
• Understanding Sales Methodologies
• Challengers & Other Animals (Different Sales personalities)
• Problems Sales Teams Can Cause Us
• Problems We Can Cause Sales Teams
• Mastering the Sales Cycle
• Understanding Win/Loss Analysis
• A Framework for Dealing with Sales-Led Feature Requests
• Defining Ideal Customer Profiles
• Leveraging Sales Enablement

* AI has made us better at shipping.

The most counter-intuitive thing about requirements is that worse is actually better.

Let that sink in.

As Product Managers we usually aim for exactly the opposite. We endlessly rewrite and polish our requirements, trying to chase perfection.

Every draft, tweak and fine-tune brings us closer to feeling proud. We carefully weigh and scrutinize every word before presenting our pristine requirements to the team.

When we finally lay out all the requirements to the team, everybody is quiet. We get zero questions and we pat ourselves on the shoulders for a job well done.

They ask zero questions, because everything is perfectly clear, right?

WRONG!

This kind of diligence is the biggest mistake you can make when formulating requirements. All this effort usually ends up in disaster by making our requirements worse in ways that are nearly impossible to detect and fix.

Why does trying to make our requirements better usually end up making them worse?

Why are gold-plated requirements worse than shoddy requirements?

How can we prevent the effort spent on formulating good requirements from backfiring?

Let’s dig in together!

<https://mdalmijn.com/p/lazy-requirements-why-worse-is-better>

:dart: Are we building the right things?
:mag: Are we building them the right way?

[Message by unknown at 391dd777-1115-5efb-93d4-d1bd872e8000]
Virality Explained

Internal Virality (Bottom-Up Adoption)
• Tally: Teams co-create forms, inviting coworkers and spreading use across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes helps more teammates join and participate.
• Slack: One invite leads to many, with team chats spreading company-wide.
• 
External Virality (New Users)
• Shortwave: External recipients of shared emails or summaries are prompted to try the product.
• Tally.so: Shared forms display Tally branding, encouraging external sign-ups.
• Asana: Task or project invites brought in external partners, expanding user base.
Viral SaaS Product Characteristics
• User-Driven Value Sharing: Product gets better as users interact/share.
• Network-Enabled Use Cases: Value increases with a connected user base.
• Built-In Triggers: Features like “invite” or “share” prompt engagement.
• Fast, Simple Onboarding: New users get up to speed and see value immediately.
• Leverages Existing Networks: Designed to help users invite their contacts.
Read more on the tactics to implement viral SaaS using Product Led Growth <https://growthwithgary.com/p/saas-virality>

*<https://open.substack.com/pub/matwinegarden/p/organizational-empathy?r=e32qu&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true|Organizational empathy> might be the most underrated skill in Product Ops.*
We talk a lot about frameworks, tooling, and processes.
We don’t talk enough about the ability to _read the room_ across the whole org.

Org empathy means you can see:
• How changes will _actually_ land with different teams
• Where friction will pop up before it’s visible in a dashboard
• When to push for change… and when to adjust your approach
Without it, even the smartest process will stall.
With it, you can design systems that stick because they work _for_ people, not just _on_ paper.

In Product Ops, org empathy isn’t “soft.”
It’s strategic.

• Where friction will pop up before it’s visible in a dashboard
• When to push for change… and when to adjust your approach

Virality Explained

Internal Virality (Bottom-Up Adoption)
• Tally: Teams co-create forms, inviting coworkers and spreading use across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes helps more teammates join and participate.
• Slack: One invite leads to many, with team chats spreading company-wide.
External Virality (New Users)

• Tally.so: Shared forms display Tally branding, encouraging external sign-ups.
• Asana: Task or project invites brought in external partners, expanding user base.

• User-Driven Value Sharing: Product gets better as users interact/share.
• Network-Enabled Use Cases: Value increases with a connected user base.
• Built-In Triggers: Features like “invite” or “share” prompt engagement.
• Fast, Simple Onboarding: New users get up to speed and see value immediately.

Ever heard of a “reverse trial” for SaaS?
Most folks know about free trials (use all the features for a week, then pay or get locked out) and freemium (use basic features for free forever). But a reverse trial flips things around for better results.

Here’s how it works:
New users start with full premium access, right away! After 7 or 30 days, if they don’t pay, they aren’t kicked out. Instead, they move to a free plan with some limits, but can still use the product and keep their work.

Why does this help?
Old way: About 15% pay after a free trial. The rest usually leave and don’t come back.
vs.
Reverse trial: 15% pay, but another 25% stick around on the free plan, which means you keep up to 40% of all signups using your tool and thinking about upgrading later.

So, instead of losing most of your trial users, you keep them close... giving them more chances to upgrade when the time is right.

Ever heard of a “reverse trial” for SaaS?
Most folks know about free trials (use all the features for a week, then pay or get locked out) and freemium (use basic features for free forever). But a reverse trial flips things around for better results.

Here’s how it works:
New users start with full premium access, right away! After 7 or 30 days, if they don’t pay, they aren’t kicked out. Instead, they move to a free plan with some limits, but can still use the product and keep their work.

Why does this help?
Old way: About 15% pay after a free trial. The rest usually leave and don’t come back.
vs.
Reverse trial: 15% pay, but another 25% stick around on the free plan, which means you keep up to 40% of all signups using your tool and thinking about upgrading later.

So, instead of losing most of your trial users, you keep them close... giving them more chances to upgrade when the time is right.

<https://growthwithgary.com/p/reverse-trial>

Get my SaaS to "Go Viral"

How Tally.so, <http://Granola.ai|Granola.ai>, Shortwave, Slack, and Asana STACKING growth with bottom-up product-led strategies and built-in virality.

*Internal virality (bottom-up adoption)*
• Tally: Teams collaborate on forms and templates, inviting coworkers to co-create and review, spreading usage across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes and summaries inside the company encourages more teammates to join and access shared knowledge.
• Slack: One person invites teammates to a channel, and soon the whole company is chatting and collaborating in real time.
*External virality (net new users)*
• Shortwave: When users send collaborative email threads or magic summaries, recipients outside the company experience the product and are prompted to try it themselves. 
• Tally.so: Every form shared externally carries Tally branding, exposing new users and making it easy for them to sign up and create their own forms. 
• Asana: Task assignments and project invites sent to external partners or clients introduce them to the platform, driving new sign-ups beyond the original organization.
*What are the Characteristics of a Viral SaaS Product?*
1. User-Driven Value Sharing - The product becomes more valuable as users interact or collaborate with others, making sharing a natural part of the workflow.
2. Network-Enabled Use Cases - The product improves when users connect with colleagues, customers, and friends who benefit from having a shared knowledge base.
3. Built-In Triggers - The product with “invite,” “share,” or “assign” artifact motivates new users to engage.
4. Fast, Simple Onboarding- New users can get started and see the value quickly, no complicated setup.
5. Uses Your Existing Network - The product is made to help you invite people you already know, so it spreads faster.
Read more on the tactics to implement viral SaaS using Product Led Growth <https://growthwithgary.com/p/saas-virality>

Get my SaaS to "Go Viral"

How Tally.so, <http://Granola.ai|Granola.ai>, Shortwave, Slack, and Asana STACKING growth with bottom-up product-led strategies and built-in virality.

*Internal virality (bottom-up adoption)*
• Tally: Teams collaborate on forms and templates, inviting coworkers to co-create and review, spreading usage across departments.
• Granola: Sharing AI meeting notes and summaries inside the company encourages more teammates to join and access shared knowledge.
• Slack: One person invites teammates to a channel, and soon the whole company is chatting and collaborating in real time.
*External virality (net new users)*
• Shortwave: When users send collaborative email threads or magic summaries, recipients outside the company experience the product and are prompted to try it themselves. 
• Tally.so: Every form shared externally carries Tally branding, exposing new users and making it easy for them to sign up and create their own forms. 
• Asana: Task assignments and project invites sent to external partners or clients introduce them to the platform, driving new sign-ups beyond the original organization.
*What are the Characteristics of a Viral SaaS Product?*
1. User-Driven Value Sharing - The product becomes more valuable as users interact or collaborate with others, making sharing a natural part of the workflow.
2. Network-Enabled Use Cases - The product improves when users connect with colleagues, customers, and friends who benefit from having a shared knowledge base.
3. Built-In Triggers - The product with “invite,” “share,” or “assign” artifact motivates new users to engage.
4. Fast, Simple Onboarding- New users can get started and see the value quickly, no complicated setup.
5. Uses Your Existing Network - The product is made to help you invite people you already know, so it spreads faster.

[Message by unknown at 7733fbf5-7c00-58be-a852-068477d99f25]
Hello Community folks:wave:,

*`Vibe-coded / no-coded a full CRM in a weekend. Here it is - I call it "SynergyFlow`*

*`What it is:`* A complete customer relationship management system with contacts, deals pipeline, activity tracking, and a dashboard. Think Salesforce, but built entirely with AI tools in days, not months.

*`Tools/Stack Used:`*

• *Prototyping:* Lovable (rapid concept visualization) :art:
• *Foundation:* v0 by Vercel (production-quality components) :building_construction:
• *Architecture:* Claude 3.5 (business logic and data relationships) :brain:
• *Refinement:* Cursor (context-aware code enhancement) :sparkles:
• *Deployment:* Vercel (instant production hosting) :globe_with_meridians:


*`How I built it:`* I did product strategy and UX thinking. AI wrote 95% of the code. I understand about 80% of it. Debugged authentication flows, data relationships, and responsive design quirks.



*`Why I built this:`*
I've been experimenting with AI-powered app builders in both work and personal projects, curious about how far we could push the "idea to working app" pipeline.

The bottleneck wasn't coding speed - it was strategic thinking. What features matter? How should data flow? What's the user journey?

*The real insight:* AI is incredible at execution, but still we need human judgment for product decisions.

*My experience building it:* <https://www.linkedin.com/posts/activity-7348199160333877249-woi8?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAC1BXpQBlnJ_NS0WET13XiUrnvQd17TLZHY|From Prompt to MVP: My 1-Hour Product Building Experience with AI & No-Code Tools>
